newsitem.title: USA: Trusted Info to export key recovery coding.
newsitem.headline: Trusted Info to export key recovery coding.

text.p: Trusted Information Systems Inc received approval from the Commerce Department to export powerful computer coding products, the company said Wednesday.

Although U.S. law generally prohibits export of strong encryption software, a new Clinton administration policy in place since Jan. 1 permits the export of such programs if the software allows the government to crack the codes.
To get the export approval, the company incorporated so-called key recovery features and designated a key recovery agent, SourceKey of Oakland, Calif.

Encrypytion programs use mathematical formulas to scramble information, such as an email message or a credit card number transmitted over the Internet, and render it unreadable without a password or software "key." Key recovery, or key escrow, products allow the government to crack the codes by gaining access to the software keys.
The security provided by encryption is largely a function of the length of the software key measure in bits, the smallest unit of computer data.
Previously all export products were limited to 40-bit long keys.

Under the latest policy, 56-bit products may be exported if the exporter agrees to incorporate key recovery features within two years. But no key length limits are imposed on exports of products that incorporate key key recovery.

Trusted Information, along with International Business Machines Corp, Digital Equipment Corp and Cylink Corp have previously acknowledged receiving permission to export 56-bit products under the two-year exemption.
But in the latest approval, Trusted Information said it had permission to export products with no key length limit.
A user outside of the United States purchasing the company's products would have to register with a key recovery agent such as SourceKey to activate the strong encryption features.
Using a two-stage process, a user would then encrypt each message with a lengthy software key and a copy of each key would be included in the messages.

The copy would be separately encrypted in a way that the government could crack by obtaining code from the key recovery agent. Once the government decoded the message's specific key, it could decode the message.

Despite the recent export approvals, many software companies complain that the current policy is too restrictive. Several bills have been introduced in Congress to substantially ease the export limits.
